summary: The Northern Arapaho are one branch of the Arapaho people. Their Southern Arapaho relatives settled in what became Oklahoma, and the Aaniiih of Montana's Fort Belknap Reservation are also kin. Northern Arapaho elders still regard the plains and mountains of northern Colorado as their historic homeland. The Oregon Trail and the Colorado gold rush brought travelers, settlers, and conflict into Arapaho country. After Colorado troops attacked a peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho village in the 1864 Sand Creek Massacre, war spread, and the northern and southern bands grew further apart. In 1868 the Northern Arapaho signed a treaty at Fort Laramie that promised them a reservation but named no place for it. For ten years they kept seeking a homeland of their own. In 1878 the government settled them, under Army escort, on the Eastern Shoshone reservation in Wyoming's Wind River Valley, and the two nations, once enemies, have shared it ever since. Today the Northern Arapaho Tribe lives mainly on the eastern side of the Wind River Reservation, with tribal offices in Ethete and Arapahoe. Royalties from oil found on tribally held land have supported members for decades.

notes: WyoHistory gives about 950 people arriving in 1878; left out as single-source. The Arapaho self-name (often written Hinono'ei) was not found on a source read this pass and is left out; the tribe's website carries almost no history, so reviewers from the Northern Arapaho community should supply the preferred self-name. The phrase about the split deepening after Sand Creek follows the Encyclopedia of the Great Plains; WyoHistory dates the north–south drift earlier, so the summary says the bands 'grew further apart.' Left out: the date royalty payments began (1940, single source) and the date the Arapaho moved onto the Plains (WyoHistory says mid-1700s per ethnohistorians; Arapaho tradition places it much earlier).
